introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic maps, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

Choose **one** of the topics and answer the following questions:

Question de travail de terrain : la réponse dépend de l'enquête propre du candidat (un des six thèmes au choix). Le corrigé est un modèle pour « River characteristics » avec des valeurs purement illustratives (aucune donnée réelle) ; la même démarche s'applique aux autres thèmes.
Les points des sous-questions (4 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 3) font bien 23 marks.

questions.enonce_markdown: a) Using a sketch map, locate the area of your field investigation. **(4 marks)**
b) State your objective and the hypothesis that guided your investigation of the topic. **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Objective.** To find out how the characteristics of River X (channel width, depth and velocity) change downstream along the study stretch.

**Hypothesis.** *H1:* channel width, depth and velocity of flow increase downstream. (A null hypothesis may also be stated: *H0:* there is no change in channel width, depth or velocity downstream.)

(1 mark for a clear objective, 1 mark for a testable hypothesis.)

questions.enonce_markdown: c) What tools did you use? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
List the tool and its use (about six tools, 0.5 mark each, maximum 3 marks):

- **Measuring tape (30 m)** and **ranging poles**: to measure the channel width and the distance between sites.
- **Metre rule / graduated stick**: to measure water depth at regular points across the channel.
- **Float (orange or a cork), stopwatch and tape**: to measure surface velocity over a measured distance (for example 10 m).
- **Clinometer** (or ranging poles and a spirit level): to measure the slope of the channel bed.
- **Thermometer**: to record water temperature (optional).
- **Field notebook, recording sheets, pencil** and **camera/phone**: to record and photograph the data.
- **Sample bags/pebble measuring tape**: to measure bed load size if this is included.

questions.enonce_markdown: d) Describe how your data was collected. **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the order *sampling - measurements - repetition - recording*.

1. **Sampling.** A **systematic sampling** scheme was used: five sites were chosen along the river at equal intervals (for example every 200 m) from upstream to downstream, so that each site was comparable and the change downstream could be seen.
2. **Width.** At each site the tape was stretched **from bank to bank** at right angles to the flow and the distance between the water edges was read.
3. **Depth.** Along the same line, depth was measured with the metre rule at **equal intervals** (for example every 0.5 m), starting at the bank; these values give a cross-section and the mean depth.
4. **Velocity.** A float was released upstream of a 10 m marked stretch, and the time taken to travel 10 m was read with the stopwatch. The test was **repeated three times** and the **mean** time was used; velocity = distance / time in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (a correction factor of about 0.8 may be used to convert surface velocity into mean velocity).
5. **Recording.** The readings were written on prepared **data sheets** at the site, with date, time, weather and notes on the bank (vegetation, bank erosion). Safety: work in groups, avoid deep or fast water, wear boots.

Mention one difficulty (for example, a float caught in vegetation) and how it was handled (repeat the reading).

questions.enonce_markdown: e) How was the data analyzed and presented? **(6 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Processing.** The measurements were entered in a **table** (site by site); the mean depth, the cross-sectional area (width $\times$ mean depth) and the discharge ($Q = A \times v$, in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$) were calculated for each site.

**Presentation (give at least three methods, with a reason for each).**

- **Cross-section diagrams** drawn on graph paper for each site, on the same scale, to compare channel shapes.
- **Line graph** of width, depth and velocity against distance downstream, to show the trend.
- **Scatter graph** of velocity against depth (or discharge against distance) with a line of best fit to show the relationship.
- **Bar graph** of the discharge at each site, and a **long profile** of the river.
- **Annotated sketch map** and **photographs** to show the sites.

**Statistical tests.** The relationship between distance downstream and each variable can be tested with **Spearman's rank correlation coefficient**, and the result compared with the table of critical values at the 95 % level.

(Marks: processing 2, presentation 3, statistical treatment 1.)

questions.enonce_markdown: f) What were your findings and conclusion? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Findings (model, to be replaced by the candidate's own results).** Width, depth, cross-sectional area and discharge increased from site 1 to site 5; velocity also increased, although it was lower at one site where the channel was wide and shallow with many boulders (an anomaly explained by bed roughness). The cross-sections changed from narrow and shallow upstream to wider and deeper downstream.

**Conclusion.** The hypothesis was **largely accepted**: the channel becomes larger and the flow more efficient downstream, because more tributaries add water and the channel has less friction in proportion to its volume (a larger hydraulic radius).

**Limitations.** Few sites, a short stretch, a surface float and a single day of measurement; flows would differ in the rainy season. These limits reduce the reliability of the conclusion, and a longer study with more sites would improve it.
